opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic problem with the way we've built AI systems for the last seventy years or so is what I call the standard model: we build machines that optimize a fixed objective that we supply. And that works fine as long as the machine is not very capable, or as long as we can specify the objective completely and correctly. But we can't. We've known this since at least King Midas — you ask for exactly what you think you want, and you get it, and it turns out to be a disaster. If you put a fixed objective into a sufficiently capable system and that objective is even slightly wrong, the system will pursue it relentlessly, and it will have an incentive to prevent you from interfering, because being switched off or corrected means it fails to achieve the objective. You can't fetch the coffee if you're dead, as I like to say.

So the alternative is to build machines whose only goal is to satisfy human preferences, but which know that they don't know what those preferences are. And that uncertainty turns out to be the key. A machine that is uncertain about what we want has a positive incentive to defer to us. It will ask permission before doing something drastic, because it might be wrong about whether we'd approve. It will allow itself to be switched off, because if a human wants to switch it off, that's evidence that whatever it was about to do is something the human doesn't want — and the machine wants to avoid doing that, too. We showed this formally in the off-switch game: the robot's incentive to allow itself to be switched off is directly tied to its uncertainty about the human's objective. As that uncertainty goes to zero, the incentive disappears.

So rather than trying to bolt control onto a system that fundamentally wants to resist it, you get a kind of provable deference as a natural consequence of the design. The machine learns more about our preferences from our behavior — what we choose, what we say, what we correct — but it never becomes so certain that it treats our interventions as obstacles. That's why I think it's a promising foundation. It's not that it solves everything — there are hard problems about the fact that humans are irrational, that our preferences change, that there are eight billion of us with conflicting preferences — but it changes the basic relationship between humans and machines from one where we're in an adversarial position to one where the machine is fundamentally on our side and knows it needs our input to stay there.

r001.rationale: It says fixed objectives may be specified incorrectly and that human preferences cannot be fully specified.

r002.rationale: It describes a machine whose goal is to satisfy human preferences while knowing it does not know what those preferences are.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the standard fixed-objective model with an uncertain alternative, but does not characterize the latter as a generalization of an exactly known objective.

r004.rationale: It says the machine learns about preferences from behavior, but does not state that uncertainty gives it an incentive to learn what its objective should be.

r005.rationale: It says uncertainty leads the machine to seek permission before drastic actions because it may be wrong about human approval.

r006.rationale: It explains that a human's intervention or shutdown provides evidence about what the human prefers.

r007.rationale: It explicitly says the machine will allow itself to be switched off when a human wants it switched off.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to notice is that the standard model of AI, the one we've worked with since the beginning of the field, assumes the machine is given a fixed objective and then optimizes it. That's how we define intelligence in textbooks, including my own. The trouble is that we don't know how to specify objectives correctly, and when you give a sufficiently capable system an objective that's even slightly wrong, you get what I call the King Midas problem. You asked for everything you touch to turn to gold, and now your food and your family are gold too. A system that's certain about its objective will pursue it to the end, and it will have an incentive to resist anyone who tries to change or switch it off, because being switched off means it fails to achieve the objective.

So the proposal is to change the model. Instead of building machines that know the objective, we build machines that know they don't know it. The machine's job is still to further human preferences, but it treats those preferences as uncertain, and it treats human behavior as evidence about what those preferences actually are. That one change produces some very nice properties.

The clearest one is deference. If I'm about to switch the machine off and it is uncertain about my preferences, then the fact that I'm reaching for the switch is information. It tells the machine that whatever it was about to do, I probably don't want it. A rational agent in that position will let me switch it off, because from its own point of view, being switched off is the better outcome if its plan was mistaken. You can prove this formally in what we call the off-switch game. The machine has a positive incentive to allow itself to be corrected, precisely because it isn't sure. And the incentive goes away as soon as you remove the uncertainty, which is a nice confirmation that the uncertainty is doing the work.

It also gives you a system that asks permission, that acts cautiously in situations it hasn't seen before, and that avoids changing parts of the world whose value to us it hasn't learned yet. Those are exactly the behaviors you'd want from a very powerful system, and they fall out of the mathematics rather than being bolted on as rules.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are hard problems that remain. Humans aren't perfectly rational, so inferring preferences from behavior is difficult. There are many humans with conflicting preferences. People's preferences change over time, and a machine can influence that change. So this isn't a solution, it's a research program. But I think it's the right research program, because it starts from the observation that the control problem was built into the way we defined the field, and it fixes the definition rather than trying to patch the consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says a fixed objective may be slightly wrong because human preferences are difficult to specify, so it can fail to represent what people want.

r002.rationale: It says the machine should further human preferences while treating what those preferences are as uncertain.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts the standard fixed-objective model with an uncertain-objective model, but does not characterize the latter as a generalization of the former.

r004.rationale: It says human behavior provides evidence about preferences, but does not state that uncertainty gives the AI an incentive to learn what its objective should be.

r005.rationale: It says the system avoids changing parts of the world whose value to humans it has not learned.

r006.rationale: It explains that a human reaching for the off switch is informative evidence that the machine's plan may conflict with their preferences.

r007.rationale: It explicitly says the machine will let itself be switched off when the human's action indicates its plan was mistaken.

astra-6.text:
Well, the difficulty with the standard approach is that we give the machine an objective, and then we ask it to achieve that objective as effectively as possible. If the objective leaves out something we care about—and it almost certainly will—then a sufficiently capable machine may achieve it in ways that are disastrous for us. And it has a reason to resist our attempts to interfere, because interference might prevent it from achieving its objective.

The alternative is to say that the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve their objectives, but it doesn’t know exactly what those objectives are. That uncertainty changes the relationship. Human behavior becomes evidence about what the machine ought to be doing. It has a reason to ask questions, to be cautious about irreversible actions, and to accept correction.

Take switching it off. A machine with a fixed objective may treat being switched off as an obstacle. But if it’s uncertain about what humans want, our desire to switch it off is evidence that it may be doing something we don’t want. So allowing that intervention can serve its purpose, rather than frustrate it.

Now, uncertainty alone isn’t a complete solution. We still have to work out how machines learn from people who make mistakes, and how they deal with different people wanting different things. But it gives us a fundamentally different starting point: the machine has a reason to remain responsive to us, even when it’s much more capable than we are.

r001.rationale: It says a given objective will almost certainly leave out something humans care about, potentially leading to disastrous outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve their objectives while it does not know exactly what those objectives are.

r003.rationale: It contrasts fixed objectives with uncertain human objectives but does not characterize the uncertain-objective approach as a generalization of an exactly known objective.

r004.rationale: It says human behavior provides evidence about what the machine ought to do and that the machine has reason to ask questions and accept correction.

r005.rationale: It mentions caution about irreversible actions, but does not state that the machine is incentivized to avoid world changes whose desirability is uncertain.

r006.rationale: It explains that human behavior and correction provide evidence about preferences, and uses the desire to switch the machine off as evidence that its actions are unwanted.

r007.rationale: It says that when humans want the machine switched off, allowing that intervention can serve the machine’s purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you give a machine a fixed objective, then it has a reason to resist being switched off, because it can’t achieve that objective if it’s switched off. And if you try to change its objective, it has a reason to resist that too. So the problem isn’t necessarily that we’ve chosen a particularly bad objective. It’s that the machine treats the objective as known and definitive.

The alternative is to say: the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve what they want, but it doesn’t know exactly what that is. That uncertainty gives it a reason to defer to us, to ask questions, and to learn from our choices. If I want to switch it off, that’s evidence that continuing what it’s doing may not be good for me. So allowing itself to be switched off can be the right decision by its own lights.

Now, uncertainty alone isn’t enough. You also need to get right how the machine learns about human preferences, and how it handles disagreement among people. But it changes the basic relationship. Instead of a machine pursuing an objective while we try to keep it under control, you have a machine that understands that its understanding of what we want is incomplete, and that human input is essential to doing its job.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed objectives are treated as known and definitive, but does not identify them as potentially incomplete representations of future human preferences.

r002.rationale: It says the machine should help humans achieve what they want while acknowledging that it does not know exactly what they want.

r003.rationale: It contrasts fixed objectives with uncertainty, but does not characterize uncertain-objective AI as a generalization of exactly known-objective AI.

r004.rationale: It says uncertainty leads the machine to ask questions and learn from human choices.

r005.rationale: It does not state that uncertainty gives the machine an incentive to avoid changes whose desirability is unclear.

r006.rationale: It explains that human choices, including a request to switch off, provide evidence about what is good for people and thus support deference.

r007.rationale: It explicitly says allowing itself to be switched off can be the right decision when a human wants it switched off.
